description: We are 2 friends who are in Computer Engineering and Information Technology Majors in Singapore who want to apply their skillsets in an actual real world problem. We are focused on the challenge Dancing with the SARs.
summary:
Tracing the Aral Sea is an interactive web atlas that connects six decades of environmental change with NISAR radar observations from June to October 2026. We developed animated satellite comparisons, water-boundary maps, an interactive classification lab, a radar-reading quiz, and charts showing changes across nine observation windows.

The project combines NISAR backscatter and interferometric coherence to investigate water extent, compares the resulting maps with Sentinel-2 optical imagery, and exposes how classification thresholds affect the results. Our analysis estimates approximately 133 km² of North Aral water retreat between the first and last observation windows, while distinguishing measured extent changes from unconfirmed causes.

Addressing “Dancing with the SARs,” the atlas turns radar data into an accessible, interactive exploration of surface change. It helps audiences understand both the Aral Sea’s history and the strengths and limitations of satellite evidence, with downloadable measurements and documented methods supporting further investigation.
details:
Tracing the Aral Sea is an interactive web atlas that combines historical satellite imagery, recent NISAR radar observations, and hands-on learning tools to explain how the Aral Sea is changing. Developed for “Dancing with the SARs,” it helps users explore surface-water changes while understanding how satellite measurements are produced and where uncertainty remains.

How it works

We processed NISAR Level-2 GCOV backscatter and GUNW interferometric coherence products from June to October 2026, focusing on the North Aral Sea and the South Aral’s western basin.

Our initial experiments showed that radar brightness alone could confuse water with exposed terrain. We therefore explored coherence, which measures the similarity of radar signals between acquisitions. Water often has low coherence, but other changing surfaces can also produce low values. Our method combines locally selected thresholds with connectivity to the lake to identify candidate open-water areas.

The workflow aligns observations to a common projected grid, extracts water boundaries, calculates areas, and compares the first and last observation windows. We also vary classification thresholds to show how sensitive the results are to methodological choices.

The completed website compares these radar-derived maps with cloud-masked Sentinel-2 imagery. Agreement and disagreement layers help users inspect differences between the two methods. These comparisons provide supporting evidence rather than proof that either classification is error-free.

Our analysis estimates approximately 133 km² of North Aral water retreat between the first and last observation windows. We distinguish this estimated extent change from water-volume change and do not attribute it to a specific cause.

What users can explore

The website includes:

  • A historical image timeline connecting recent observations with decades of change.
  • Animated radar observations and water-boundary overlays.
  • A “Spot the Water” quiz demonstrating the difficulty of interpreting radar brightness.
  • An interactive threshold lab where users adjust the classification and watch the mapped area change.
  • Radar–optical swipe and lens comparisons.
  • Area charts, threshold-sensitivity ranges, downloadable measurements, and an evidence ledger separating observations, published reports, and future plans.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes satellite analysis accessible to students, educators, and people interested in water management. It connects environmental storytelling with inspectable evidence, encouraging users to ask how a map was made before accepting its conclusions.

Its intended impact is to improve understanding of surface-water monitoring and demonstrate a reproducible approach that could be adapted to other lakes. It is an exploratory research and communication tool, rather than an operational water-management system.

Tools and technologies

We used Python, with NumPy, h5py, Rasterio, SciPy, Shapely, Pillow, and Matplotlib, for data processing, spatial analysis, and visualization. QGIS and GDAL supported geospatial inspection and exports. The website uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, including browser-based graphics and interactions, without a frontend framework or build step. Data came from NASA Earthdata/ASF, Copernicus Sentinel-2, and historical NASA/USGS imagery.

Creativity and team considerations

Our central creative choice was to let visitors investigate the evidence themselves. The quiz exposes interpretation challenges; the threshold lab reveals how analytical decisions affect boundaries; and the optical comparison makes disagreements visible.

Throughout development, we considered acquisition gaps, clouds, surface conditions, spatial resolution, classification sensitivity, and the difference between seasonal variation and long-term change. We also considered accessibility, including reduced-motion behavior, and kept methods and measurements available for further scrutiny.
